item.title: INSTRUCTION: A Beautiful Cabbage Galette
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried). For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub. Need to make a substitution? - CrustStep 1Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain). Step 2Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using. - Filling and AssemblyStep 3When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside. Step 4Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool. Step 5Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine. Step 6Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet. Step 7Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.) Step 8Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving. Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

item.title: Delta expands again in Austin focus city, adds new route to Walmart's backyard
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.” Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville. Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet. The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA. The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas. For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin. The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.” That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April. That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico. All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer. In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS. “The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub. “We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.” It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters. Delta's Austin-Northwest Arkansas route details As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7. It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8. The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest. “This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday. Delta, Southwest both have big plans in Austin While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport. Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027. Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years. By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too. This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA). item.title: INSTRUCTION: Thanksgiving Cornbread
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make. The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly. For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl. Step 2Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Step 3Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan. Step 4Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter. Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

item.title: REVIEW: My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay. I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights. Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after. Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy. Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn. Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame. The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months. Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio. item.title: SALES: 12 Travel Audiobooks for Your Next Adventure
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
When you want the best travel audiobooks to survive transit delays, you need plots that hold up through interruptions and voices that stay clear. This guide mixes travel memoirs, adventure writing, reflective essays, and family listening so you can match a book to your exact transit style. Before downloading media for offline travel, also check legal listening options. For example, using platforms like Audiobook Bay, often abbreviated as ABB, can be risky because torrent sites can carry malware that poses inherent security risks. Because anyone can upload a file to the network, bad actors can easily hide. Secure solutions help you know where files come from before you download them. Once sorted, the fun part is choosing what belongs in your headphones! 1. 'Wild' by Cheryl Strayed: Save It for a Long Solo Journey The Pacific Crest Trail stretches across thousands of miles of wilderness, offering plenty of time for intense contemplation. Strayed documents her solo trek following personal loss, forming a narrative that works well for a traveler spending several uninterrupted hours alone. Download the audiobook before you risk losing reliable internet access at the trailhead. Wild fits a long solo trip with several hours for one continuous story. Penguin Random House lists it at 13 hours and 3 minutes, so it also works well across several travel days. 2. 'A Walk in the Woods' by Bill Bryson: Take Humor Onto a Hiking Trip Bill Bryson sets out to walk the Appalachian Trail with his friend Stephen Katz, whom the publisher describes as out of shape at the start. The book mixes their trail experience with Bryson's observations about its history and the people they meet along the way. This format suits a travel day when you want a book you can leave and return to without a dense plot. The humor comes from the mismatch between the Appalachian Trail's scale and how prepared the hikers feel once the trip starts. 3. 'In Patagonia' by Bruce Chatwin: Hear a Place Through Fragments Bruce Chatwin builds In Patagonia from encounters, historical episodes, and stories collected during his trip through southern South America. Penguin describes the book as a travel account filled with history and anecdotes, giving it a fragmented structure that works well for shorter listening sessions. The 2019 Penguin Audio edition is narrated by Hugh Fraser. It suits a train journey or trip, with frequent pauses, since the book moves through separate people and episodes rather than one continuous plot. Rocinante is the name of the custom pickup truck Steinbeck uses to cross America with his standard poodle, Charley. They look for the country's real character in the autumn of 1960. Crossing multiple state lines in a day calls for a book whose geography matches your motion. The road unfolds through the speakers as the highway stretches ahead of your windshield. 5. 'West With the Night' by Beryl Markham: Travel Through East Africa From the Cockpit Beryl Markham grew up in East Africa, trained racehorses, and became a bush pilot in the 1930s. In 1936, she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic from east to west, a flight that became one of the defining episodes of her memoir. That aviation history gives the audiobook a natural place on a long flight. Listening to Markham describe early flying in East Africa while traveling in a modern aircraft illustrates the difference between those two kinds of air travel. 6. 'The Art of Travel' by Alain de Botton: Airport Downtime Gets a Philosophical Check Alain de Botton examines what people expect from travel and why the reality can feel different once a trip begins. He writes about anticipation, disappointment, airports, and how travelers carry their existing worries even when the destination changes. That makes The Art of Travel a good fit for an airport wait or long connection. A departure lounge gives you time to listen to his observations about anticipation while living through that part of a trip. 7. 'Vagabonding' by Rolf Potts: Listen While Planning a Longer Trip Extended travel requires sound financial planning and a mindset shift away from standard vacation habits. Potts breaks down how to take months off to explore the world on a modest budget. Listening during initial trip prep or the first flight helps anchor your expectations. Dave Lee built Go Backpacking from years of independent travel through dozens of countries, making this philosophy a natural fit for readers planning departures. 8. 'The Geography of Bliss' by Eric Weiner: Let Each Country Reset the Listening Rhythm Weiner visits Iceland, India, Switzerland, and other nations to ask how different cultures define and pursue happiness. Each chapter focuses on one place, giving the book an episodic rhythm. A backpacker on a regional train can finish a country profile without following a massive plotline. The unabridged Hachette Audio edition is read by Weiner himself. Its place-by-place structure works well for travel days when you expect to pause between listening sessions. 9. 'Lands of Lost Borders' by Kate Harris: Pair Cycling Travel With Big-Distance Writing Kate Harris recounts a bicycle journey along the Silk Road with her childhood friend Mel Yule. The travel memoir follows their journey through remote regions as Harris also writes about borders and what exploration means once most of the world has already been mapped. For cyclists, the book fits naturally into the quieter parts of a trip. You can listen after reaching camp or during a rest day, when the physical distance covered in the book clearly connects to your own journey. Phileas Fogg makes a famous wager to circumnavigate the globe in record time. The constant change of scenery keeps younger passengers engaged during long stretches of highway. Finding the best audiobooks for family travel requires a clear narrative and simple geographic milestones everyone in the car can track. The story moves through countries and transportation changes while the deadline stays fixed from the start. Penguin lists one current edition for readers ages 10 and up, which makes the story a reasonable option for families with older children. The clear objective also gives everyone in the car an easy question to follow: will Fogg make it back to London on time? 11. 'Born To Run' by Christopher McDougall: Use a Travel Day for an Endurance Story Christopher McDougall travels to Mexico's Copper Canyon to learn about the Tarahumara, a society known for long-distance running. The book combines his reporting with the story of ultrarunning and the physical demands behind endurance. That makes it a good fit for a longer train ride or travel day when you want nonfiction tied to movement and place. To check main ideas before the full audiobook, Headway includes Born to Run in its travel collection as a summary you can read or listen to during a shorter connection. Travel downtime can also be a chance to learn new subjects through the best microlearning apps, which offer short lessons that fit between connections or during a break from exploring. 12. 'The Hobbit' by J.R.R. Tolkien: Give the Whole Car One Common Adventure Groups traveling together need a single story that appeals to different tastes after a long drive. Bilbo Baggins leaves his comfortable hobbit hole and steps into a structured quest with clear stages. The Hobbit has that framework. Bilbo leaves home, joins a quest, and moves through distinct stages easy to pick up after a break. This expands top travel audiobooks beyond memoirs into shared fictional landscapes. HarperCollins publishes an unabridged audiobook narrated by Andy Serkis. Match the Audiobook to the Trip You Are Taking The best travel audiobooks depend on the part of the journey that needs filling. A long solo route suits Wild. A driving day fits Travels with Charley. Family travel works better with a story everyone can rejoin after a stop, like Around the World in Eighty Days or The Hobbit. Long-term backpackers may get more from Vagabonding. A quiet train suits The Art of Travel. Check the longest uninterrupted stretch in your itinerary and choose the audiobook whose structure and runtime fit that part of the trip! This story was published in partnership with Headway.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Gravy-Braised Turkey
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy. This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself. For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.) Step 2Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly). Step 3Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper. Step 4Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes. Step 5Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Simple-Is-Best Stuffing
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.” Watch Carla make Simple-Is-Best Stuffing The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter. Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner. What’s the best bread for this stuffing? Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old. Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered? The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center. Can I make this stuffing ahead of time? Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead. What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing? Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl. Step 2Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool. Step 3Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes. Step 4Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer. Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes. Editor’s note: We first published this Thanksgiving stuffing recipe in our November 2012 issue as ‘Simple Is Best Dressing’; it has been updated for style. item.title: IDEA: I Escaped Zion’s Crushing Crowds at Red Cliffs, a Desert Dupe Just 45 Minutes Away
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
I just wanted one picture of my son without a sea of people in the background. We were hiking The Narrows in Zion National Park, a bucket-list adventure that has you wading for miles through knee-deep water in the belly of a canyon. It’s awesome. It’s also crowded. And getting a photo to commemorate the adventure without a bunch of strangers in it was proving to be difficult. Crowds are simply a fact of life when it comes to visiting Zion, which has skyrocketed in popularity over the last 20 years, doubling its visitation rates from 2.5 million in 2005 to almost five million in 2025. That’s a lot of people to squeeze into Zion’s 146,597 acres, so you’re going to have company on your hike. Fortunately, there’s an alternative nearby. Red Cliffs National Conservation Area is less than an hour west of Zion National Park with a desert landscape that’s just as stunning but only attracts a fraction of the crowds. Red Cliffs National Conservation Area is about 45,000 acres, which is less than a third of the size of Zion. But the smaller size is a bonus here. Since you won’t have to navigate mandatory shuttles or shift your plans to avoid crowds, the compact size of the park allows you to knock out a variety of adventures in a short amount of time. And there is an amazing variety of adventures inside Red Cliffs, which is packed with sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and miles of slickrock, all of which are traversed by more than 100 miles of developed trails. The area is managed by the Bureau of Land Management, so don’t expect visitor centers or rangers on hand. This is a raw desert landscape that’s set aside for you to explore on your own. Once you get inside the conservation area, keep your eyes out for some unique wildlife, most notably Gila monsters and a rare species of desert tortoise. I spent two days exploring Red Cliffs with my son during a recent trip to southern Utah, and it made me want to go back for more. Here’s a first-timer’s guide to exploring Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. If you’re only going to do one trail in Red Cliffs, this is it. And I’m using the word “trail” loosely here. Sometimes called the Red Cliffs Nature Trail, Red Reef does in fact start out as a mild walk through a picnic area, but quickly gets interesting as it delivers you into the heart of a slot canyon. The three-mile out-and-back is more of a choose-your-own-adventure as you move across the sandy desert floor into a slickrock canyon that gets increasingly narrow as you move deeper into its belly. There’s some light scrambling involved, with one fixed rope that you’ll need to use to get around a small waterfall. And be prepared to get wet; there are a few pockets of deep water in the narrowest channels that were up to my chest. You can turn around if it gets too deep, though. The rock outcroppings just outside of the canyon are also fun to scramble and explore after you’ve navigated to the end of the canyon. It’s an ideal slot canyon experience for first-time canyoners, and you’ll probably have it all to yourself once you climb past that first waterfall. Moab is known as ground zero for slickrock, but the town doesn’t hold a monopoly on the grippy rock surface. This 7.5-mile loop is mostly slickrock with the occasional singletrack connector. The loop has steep climbs, the occasional sandy wash, and plenty of long-range views of the surrounding sandstone cliffs. Keep an eye out for prehistoric dinosaur tracks—along Dino Cliffs Trail you’ll find 17 well-preserved tracks left by meat-eating theropods during the Jurassic period. Snow Canyon State Park is its own pocket destination with 7,400 acres of cliffs, petrified dunes and black lava rock, located within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve. The majority of the trails are short, making the park the perfect one-day adventure. You’re going to want to hit the Petrified Sand Dunes Trail, which traverses rolling humps of hardened sandstone. It’s a 1.2-mile out-and-back, but you can spend some time exploring this wild beach of petrified sand. Just be sure you leave yourself enough time to explore the Lava Flow Trail, a one-mile out-and-back that traverses a black lava flow that cuts through the center of the park. You’ll get views of the surrounding tan cliffs as you hike, but the real joy of this trail is ducking into the three lava tubes, a couple of which you can scramble into and spend some time poking around beneath the surface of the desert floor (bring a headlamp). Red Cliffs even has an arch. It’s not a particularly large arch—just 10 feet wide and eight feet tall—but it’s tucked into a beautiful expanse of sandstone outcroppings hovering above the Virgin River. Combine a series of trails from the Sand Cove trailhead for a 2.2-mile out-and-back that traverses sandy singletrack, slickrock, and a steep sand dune to reach the arch. There’s also a side trail that leads down to the Virgin River if you want to take a dip. Like most trails in Red Cliffs, it’s as much fun to explore the rock formations surrounding the path as it is to hike to the destination. Red Cliffs has portions of two federally designated Wilderness areas within its borders. The standout of the two is Red Mountain Wilderness, an 18,700-acre slice of desert that sits just north of Snow Canyon State Park. The Red Mountain Trail is a 12.8-mile out-and-back that traverses the wilderness with a trailhead that’s just off of Highway 18. No need to hike the full trail though; knock out the first 2.3 miles and you’ll climb from a sandy desert with sagebrush and pinyon pines into the sandstone outcroppings where Red Mountain Overlook delivers an amazing view of Snow Canyon and the St. George valley below. Red Cliffs has two campgrounds, the developed Red Cliffs Campground, which has 11 sites with shade structures that will put you within walking distance of the Red Reef Trail ($15 per night, reservations available six months in advance) and the tougher-to-reach Sand Cove Campground, a primitive, backcountry group campground with room for 20 people that’s only accessible by 4WD vehicle (free, but permit required). If you camp at Sand Cove, you’ll have immediate access to the one-mile out-and-back Anasazi Valley Trail (or Tempi’po’op Trail), which leads to well-preserved ruins of the Puebloans that once called this area home. Beer: The town of St. George is just 15 minutes away so post-adventure beers and food are readily available. Silver Reef Brewing Co. is known for its barrel-aged beers, which might not be what you’re looking for after a day in the desert, but they have great lagers too, as well as a kitchen pumping out pizzas and wings. Best Season: Fall through spring for mild temperatures. Graham Averill is Outside magazine’s national parks columnist. He doesn’t mind a crowd, but understands the value of standing in the middle of the desert all alone.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: A Classic Thanksgiving Menu With Make-Ahead Tips
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
The editors at Bon Appétit take Thanksgiving very seriously. We are, in fact, in the business of furnishing readers with rigorously tested dishes destined for your family’s annual holiday table (and hopefully—eventually!—the treasured recipe box). What we’ve learned over the years is that—no matter how adventurous a cook might be 364 days of the year—when it comes to T-Day, most people don’t really budge from their traditional mainstays. People often crave a classic, tried-and-true holiday meal. Guests expect it. So we’re happy to share this menu of Thanksgiving favorites from our archives to get you to the Rockwellian holiday spread of your dreams. These are the dishes we wait all year for: roast turkey and gravy, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, stuffing, cranberry sauce, buttery rolls, and pumpkin pie. Plus a few tips for making elements ahead. You’d be hard-pressed to conjure up a more quintessential bird than our 2017 covergirl. This whole-roasted, beautifully burnished Thanksgiving turkey gets a straightforward dry brine, keeping the white meat succulent and juicy. You can’t beat Andy Baraghani’s make-ahead gravy, which you can prepare up to four days ahead. Reheat it with a bit of stock to revive that perfectly silky texture. This recipe, originally published as “Ultra-Creamy Mashed Potatoes” in our 2017 Thanksgiving spread, includes its own list of not-to-miss tips for superior mashed potatoes. They’re so good, in fact, they retroactively earned the mantle of BA’s Best. Make sure you know where you’ve stashed the ricer (or food mill). My colleague Chris Morocco probably didn’t expect his 2016 recipe to become the gold standard for green bean casserole. Yet it’s held that title year after year. No canned cream of mushroom soup here—the savory sauce is totally D.I.Y. The French’s Crispy Fried Onions, however, aren’t going anywhere. The people have spoken: Victoria Granof’s 2012 stuffing recipe gets virtually dog-eared every Thanksgiving. It’s minimalist but has everything you expect from stuffing (technically “dressing” as it’s cooked outside of the turkey in its own casserole dish), including the quintessential quartet of herbs: parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme. Making cranberry sauce is the first order of business on my Thanksgiving menu. I usually whip up a batch of Priya Krishna’s 2019 version the weekend before and feel an outsized sense of pride that I’ve managed to tick one thing off the long prep list. Her recipe is a great starting (or ending) point, but you can jazz it up with a cinnamon stick, star anise, or a few cranks of black pepper if you’d like. Or sub in brown sugar for white—the choice is yours! Try not to fill up on these buttery treasures before The Big Meal. Originally published in the iconic Fannie Farmer Baking Book, we featured these as part of our 2012 Thanksgiving menu in print. You can bake them ahead of time, let them cool, and keep them in the freezer for reheating. Or, if you’re feeling a little adventurous, try their distant cousin, Salt Bread, for even more oohs and ahhs. Is it even Thanksgiving without pumpkin pie? Rick Martinez’s 2016 rendition is as classic as they come, and it tastes even better the next day (if you’re lucky enough to have any leftovers… come to think of it, maybe just plan on making two?). You don’t have to cook the whole menu on Thanksgiving morning. Here’s what you can get out of the way: Remember to account for oven space on Thanksgiving itself: The green bean casserole still needs baking, the stuffing needs its final uncovered bake, and the rolls need warming. Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

item.title: SALES: The top travel specialists to know right now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When we created our inaugural list of the top travel specialists last year, it was based on the belief that they’re more crucial than ever. In an age of Web3, artificial intelligence, and vast warehouses of digital information on nearly every destination imaginable, we need them. Not just to guide us to the heart of a place, avoiding lazy tropes and opening doors that would otherwise remain locked, but to make sure we do so with due sensitivity to local environments and communities. A year on, with the likes of ChatGPT making even more of an impact, that belief remains unchanged and firmer than ever. So, we’ve spent the past months at Conde Nast Traveller slowly growing our list of top UK-facing travel specialists. According to James Jayasundera, who has run tailor-made specialists Ampersand Travel for more than two decades, there are both practical and emotional reasons for the very human role of a travel specialist. “The world is changing so fast, and more people are travelling based on something they’ve seen online or on an Instagram reel,” he says. “You need a really informed guide to explain both the reality of what you’ll see, and its impact; to manage expectations, but also to guide you towards something that might be even better.” Jayasundera has travelled extensively since he was a child, initially with his English mother and Sri Lankan diplomat father. Now, he doesn’t just have one of the most far-reaching little black books in the business (especially on Sri Lanka and India), but also a very global context: meaning he can tell you how the Himalayas might compare to the Andes or the Dolomites, or the nuances of Asian versus African safaris. He says Ampersand trips are also about compassion, and often sensitivity to very specific needs – from a 75-year-old woman who wanted to learn to swim with her granddaughter to a terminally ill woman who knew that her trip to southern Sri Lanka with her husband would be her last, and passed away happy and at peace on the flight home from Colombo. That humanity sums up our list of travel specialists, which now has nine new additions. They include global all-rounders like Carrier and Crossing Travel, as well as companies with a laser-like regional focus, such as Selective Asia, founded by Nick Pulley after living in Thailand and extensively travelling through its surrounding countries, and Mahlatini Luxury Travel, known for its trips to Africa and the Indian Subcontinent. We’ve also picked travel specialists such as ski expert Powder Byrne and Kirker Holidays, which organises cultural city breaks in Europe. They join other operators with a finely carved niche, including The Slow Cyclist, founded by round-the-world biker Oli Broom, flight-free experts Byway, and Inclusive Morocco, which offers magical trips that address specific destination challenges, especially for LGBTQ+ travellers. All these brands trade in the unGoogleable: the local party fixer, the world-expert guide, the secret diving spot, access to the after-hours museum or gallery, sometimes with the artist; they can find the exact villa for your exact needs, or create the bucket list trip that doesn’t just exceed your expectations but explodes them, leaving you transformed. Enjoy our list of trusted travel specialists – and happy travels. Best for: Destination weddings, honeymoons and milestone celebrations; design-led journeys across Europe and worldwide Key destinations: Japan, India, Italy, Peru, Africa; bespoke journeys across Europe, Asia and the Americas Signature trip: Japan and South Korea – ryokans, temples, artisans & architecture Also Try: Switzerland's Medical and Wellness Retreat Launched in 2013, the London-based Crossing Travel is an international team working across time zones. Founder Sangeeta Sadarangani's strength lies in her little black book and 24/7 service – whether it's resolving a flight disruption in Tokyo at 3am or securing an impossible-to-book restaurant reservation in Paris. Her company has grown mainly through word of mouth (95 per cent of new clients arrive by referral), with one-of-a-kind journeys across all seven continents, from Peru to India (where one client tried his hand at making rotis for visitors at Bangla Sahib Gurdwara in New Delhi). The “Celebrations by Crossing” service specialises in organising destination weddings, from 15-guest gatherings to 150-person events; it includes seamless luxury hotel blocks for weddings and bespoke activities such as chef's-table dinners, yacht days, and perfume-making ateliers. Best for: Bespoke ultra-luxury travel, extraordinary celebrations and personalised adventures Key destinations: The Alps, France, Austria, Italy, British Virgin Islands, bespoke journeys worldwide Signature trip: Michelin-starred dining experience on a remote glacier above Verbier Also try: Private island takeovers and superyacht expeditions ALS Private, renowned for pushing the limits of possibility in ultra-luxury travel and events for private clients and global corporations. Founded in 2013 by former professional skier Bella Syme, the company's story began in the Alps, where it built a reputation for providing unparalleled ski and chalet experiences. ALS Private has now expanded its portfolio to include a collection of properties and meticulously curated experiences on land and at sea in destinations as varied as Courchevel, Mustique, and Lapland. Describing part of its mission as turning the "impossible into reality", the company provides access to unique and exclusive villas, superyachts, private islands, and hotel buyouts for high-net-worth families, celebrities, and corporate firms worldwide. Best for: Tailor-made journeys to lesser-explored corners of the world Key destinations: Nordics, Baltics, Balkans, Caucasus, Southeast Asia, Far East Also try: Faroe Islands Fly-Drive Adventure Noel Cairns formed Regent in 1970 after travelling through the Balkans and Turkey – then unusual destinations for UK visitors – and wanted to arrange similarly unconventional holidays for others. Regent Holidays became the first UK operator to offer tours to Albania before expanding to destinations like Belarus, Central Asia, North Korea and the Baltic states. Today, the company uses trusted relationships with local partners to create personalised tours to some of the most extraordinary, remote and unconventional destinations in the world, curated by its knowledgeable and hands-on team. Key destinations: Europe, South Africa, East Africa, North America, Caribbean Signature trip: Under the spell of Sicily Born from its roots as Africa specialists, today, Carrier’s nearly 90-strong team arranges holidays to over 75 countries. Personalised experiences, private access, and intricate itineraries involving complex logistics are all USPs – whether that involves sourcing a Peloton for a superyacht or arranging a private dinner with Nelson Mandela’s former prison guard. Key to it all is the company’s long-established on-the-ground partnerships with DMCs who will go the extra mile (think asking a National Geographic producer to join a safari in India for photography enthusiast guests). Collections such as Running Wild, a series of immersive wildlife journeys, are designed for individuals who want to make a positive impact through community engagement and conservation. Key destinations: Caribbean, Indian Ocean, Europe, Asia & Australasia. Signature trip: Ultimate Caribbean Island Hopping Adventure Founded in 1974, ITC Travel Group is one of the oldest specialist travel groups in the UK. What began as a Caribbean holiday specialist has since grown into a collection of brands that span the globe, offering highly personalised, experience-led travel based on first-hand destination knowledge and expertise. Its broad portfolio includes African and Latin American wildlife specialist Rainbow Tours; the Inspiring Travel Company, which specialises in high-end tailor-made holidays; and Regent Holidays, the experts on tailor-made journeys to lesser-explored corners of the world. Key destinations: Africa, Europe, Asia, North America, Australasia Born in 1986 out of Andrew Dunn’s desire to revolutionise ski holidays for the luxury traveller, this global tour operator specialises in high-end holidays, whether clients are wanting the finest private chalet in the Alps, a remote safari lodge in the Okavango Delta or an expedition cruise to Antarctica. The immersive, seamlessly-run Explorer Kids Clubs in destinations such as Greece and Courchevel 1650 are next-level, looking after children from as young as 4 months old to teens; the Scott Dunn Private network focuses on bespoke travel, one-of-a-kind experiences (such as rare access to the Vatican Archives; teeing off at Augusta National with a former golfing champion) and access to everything from insider storytellers to private castles and yacht charters. Best for: Bespoke, tailor-made journeys with rare access Key destinations: Kenya, Japan, India, Argentina, South Africa Signature trip: Luxury Kenya: Exclusive safari + beach Also try: Japan's Hidden Gems: Two Week Japan Itinerary With a shared background working in Botswana’s safari industry, Henrietta Loyd and Susie Cazenove decided to band together in 1993 to create journeys for clients throughout east and southern Africa (Christopher Wilmot-Sitwell joined later, launching the Latin America and Asia divisions). Today, cazenove+loyd covers seven regions of the world, from Kenya and Brazil to Oman’s Dhofar Province and the islands of the Pacific. In each, its travel experts draw on first-hand knowledge and close relationships with the people on the ground, gaining access to spectacular places and private properties. One months-in-the-planning trip for a client to Papua New Guinea, for instance, was based around them spending time with several seldom-visited communities, including the Huli Wigmen of Tari and the Kasua people. Key trips: African safaris, Europe, Asia and South America Founded by prolific traveller Henry Morley in 2013, True Travel now runs bespoke trips to every continent except North America, with a focus on service and details – and a particular expertise in family trips, from organising Junior Rangers programmes in South Africa to teenage treasure hunts around the Greek islands. “Everything we do is about in-depth destination expertise and service,” says Morley. “In a world where technology is all-consuming, our clients deserve exceptional human service" says Morley. “If your flight is cancelled at 2am, we will fix it before you wake up. We’ll book you in Room Four over Room Eight, because we’ve been there, and we know.” True Travel is also a B Corp, offering clients the chance to offset double their trip’s carbon emissions, and with a foundation working on everything from seagrass rewilding in Scotland to female empowerment programmes in Zambia. Key destinations: Maldives, Mauritius, South Pacific, New Zealand and Australia Signature trip: Australia travel itinerary: Station and Tropical Island Life When husband-and-wife James and Sue Bell, together with Brian Barton, started Turquoise over two decades ago, they identified Tahiti as an untapped destination for honeymoons – which instantly became their speciality. This was later followed by family travel and once-in-a-lifetime trips such as a recent itinerary that encompassed gorilla trekking in Rwanda, safari in Kenya, Botswana and South Africa, and a beach hideaway in Mozambique. Nothing is sold that hasn’t been seen by one of the team (in 2024 they visited over 300 hotels between them) and concepts such as “50 Rooms or Less” which cater to demand from clients seeking out truly authentic places to stay. Key destinations: India, Kenya, Ecuador, Botswana Signature trip: West Papua and Asmat tribe expedition Also try: Andes to the Amazon self-drive Over 30 years ago, Nick Laing was in the foothills of the Altai Mountains in southern Russia (part of the Great Steppe), listening to folk music and gazing out across the landscape, when he had a lightbulb moment: that others might like to see such remote parts of the world too. Fast-forward to now and B Corp-certified Steppes Travel crafts epic safaris and far-flung cultural journeys. Behind-the-scenes access and unique experiences are a trademark – whether clients are viewing a private Mughal art collection, rhino darting in South Africa or staying in a tented camp as part of a hosted group tour to the Kumbh Mela in India, the largest religious gathering in the world. Key destinations: India, Kenya, South Africa, Japan, Australia Also try: Canada: In Search of Spirit Bears Although The Ultimate Travel Company specialises in tailor-made journeys and small group tours to over 100 countries, the roots of its two directors are in adventure travel. Nick van Gruisen and Rowan Paterson worked as professional guides in Africa and the Himalayas respectively, before setting up Worldwide Journeys & Expeditions, which merged with The Ultimate Travel Company in 2003. A trusted global network of on-the-ground partners opens doors to remote bear lodges in British Columbia, safari camps in Botswana and desert retreats in Chile’s Atacama. Closer to home, the company arranges European weekends shaped around art, food and culture, from Bilbao’s Guggenheim to the palazzos of Venice. Key destinations: Brazil, New Zealand, Botswana, Vietnam, Indonesia, Italy When George Morgan-Grenville founded Red Savannah in 2011, his priority was client-first service and crafting private journeys everywhere from Africa to Indonesia. What makes Red Savannah stand out are its superb specialists, who each have deep-rooted connections and years of experience in their region, meaning they know the best naturalist in Australia, or which guide in Chile suits a family with younger children, or they can find a last-minute chef for a special birthday lunch in New Zealand. A handpicked selection of charter gulets and yachts, and luxury villas in France, Italy, Greece, Spain and the Caribbean are also on their books. Key destinations: Antarctica, Galapagos, Iceland, Kenya, Norway Signature trip: Antarctica by superyacht and submersible Also try: Aurora domes: our luxury Iceland camp Henry Cookson’s next-level expeditions – such as winning the Polar Challenge race to the Magnetic North Pole in 2005 – were the inspiration behind Cookson Adventures, which he launched 19 years ago. The company creates (and often hosts) around four built-from-scratch, carbon-neutral adventures a month, typically incorporating superyachts, helicopters, submersibles and camps in places where there is little infrastructure such as the Namib desert in Angola or the rainforest in Papua New Guinea. Frontline access to conservation is key: recent expeditions have helped translocate 26 elephants from Namibia to Angola, collar lions in Mozambique and research whales off Svalbard. Key destinations: Southeast Asia, Japan, North America, South America, Australasia, African safari, India, Italy Also try: Cape Town, Kruger and Victoria Falls When Audley was founded in 1996 (then under the name Asian Journeys), co-founder Craig Burkinshaw had already been offering small-group tours to Vietnam, having fallen in love with the country as a backpacker in the early 1990s. The company offered a new type of travel: individual journeys, designed to match the traveller’s passions and preferences. This tailor-made ethos has remained key to the brand, even as it’s grown to become one of the bigger UK-based travel brands, covering more than 80 destinations. Audley still offers deep personalisation, though, beginning trips by asking travellers how they want to feel, rather than what they want to see. It aims to connect people to their destinations on a much more resonant level: for example, sorting a Delhi, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan trip for a keen photographer, from the sunrise at Agra to the blue buildings of Jodhpur’s Old Town. Or even helping families find the villages where their émigré grandparents lived. Key destinations: Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Japan, Peru Geoffrey Kent grew up on a farm in Kenya and, together with his parents, set up Abercrombie & Kent in 1962 to pioneer luxury safari travel. Now the tour operator has one of the largest in-house DMC networks in the world, whose in-depth local knowledge and meticulous attention to detail is behind each of the tailor-made trips it arranges to over 100 countries. Small-group journeys (some of the most far-flung led by Kent himself), expedition cruises and private jet adventures are also key areas of expertise. Sister company Abercrombie & Kent Philanthropy focuses on initiatives in education, healthcare and conservation. Started by Alex Malcolm in 2008 who wanted to showcase a lesser-seen side to Brazil, Jacada Travel now designs one-of-a-kind journeys across all seven continents and 80 countries (since 2020, it has also been part of Wilderness Safaris). Driven by a commitment to purpose-led travel, Jacada pairs expert specialists with an in-country concierge team that can deliver extraordinary access – travellers might find themselves visiting Queen Nefertari's tomb or standing beneath the Sistine Chapel at dawn with the Vatican keyholder. The company’s Positive Impact Collection has a selection of rigorously vetted properties and experiences, chosen for their transformational impact not only on the destination or host communities, but on the travellers themselves. Key destinations Nepal, Italy, Kenya, Mongolia, Greece Raised by nomadic parents, for Alice Daunt a career in travel was just about inevitable. She has been in the industry for nearly 30 years, setting up her agency just over a decade ago (she describes her approach as “a personal touch with a sense of adventure”), to create individual trips for clients – whether they are seeking out the road less travelled in Chad or a weekend in Venice. She is always uncovering overlooked corners and has access to private homes that few others have on their books. “We are suited to people who are as happy eating at the best table in a three-star Michelin restaurant as they are having a picnic in a bucolic setting on a summer’s day,” she says. Key destinations: Iceland, Scotland, Norway, New Zealand, Kenya, Morocco Signature trip: New Zealand Beyond Boundaries Also try: Morocco experiences inspired by Mission Impossible Few founders can fuse top-end travel with proper adventure quite like Geordie Mackay Lewis and Jimmy Carroll, two former British Army captains who founded Pelorus in 2017, using many of the skills they learned on long-range desert patrols and helicopter operations. While the focus is on bespoke global adventures planned with military precision, the team are also seriously connected, so can organise everything from stays at Scottish distillers’ private manor houses (with access to distilleries not open to the market) to learning stunt choreography with the Mission Impossible teams. Pelorus Yachting organises next-level charters from the fjords to the Falklands, while Pelorus Aviation runs private journeys via helicopter, private jet and group plane charters. The family service offers trips inspired by the imagination of the children, such as sleeping in a futuristic airstream camper and meeting a real-life astronaut. Key destinations: The Caribbean, Indian Ocean, the Med, Southeast Asia Signature trip: The Many Faces of North America | Luxury Cruise Also try: Wildlife, Wilderness and Wellness in British Columbia Geoff Moss and Barbara Catchpole launched Elegant in 1988 with top-end trips to the Caribbean and especially Barbados on Concorde. While the postcard-worthy Caribbean remains a key focus (there’s still an office in Barbados), the brand has expanded across the world – not just a network of the best hotels and experiences, but a concierge team that can add bespoke flourishes and secure in-demand reservations. Recent examples of going the extra mile include organising a surprise proposal for a regular client’s granddaughter at the Summit One Vanderbilt overlooking the New York skyline. Founded in 1999 by the ever-immaculate Amanda Teale, Minerva Private has kept its network tight and exclusive ever since. There’s hardly any information on the website, and they’re notoriously tight-lipped about releasing specific details of their offerings. Clients come by referral, knowing that Teale and her small team can arrange the impossible. Key destinations: Morocco, Japan, Iceland, Argentina, Chile, Italy, US Also try: Tokyo and Kyoto: A Japan Family Holiday When they launched in Shoreditch in 2005, Tom Marchant, James Merrett and Matt Smith named their brand after the sweet, juicy black tomatoes of Russia – and their MO has been to bust travel’s “same-same” status quo ever since. As well as bespoke global trips that prioritise local community access, the team specialise in attention-grabbing itineraries like their high-end TV-inspired jaunts, including Yellowstone and Ripley; or family trips based on children’s stories, such as Alice in Wonderland in which the kids have tea parties and go on treasure hunts in the Oxfordshire countryside. Key destinations: South Africa, the Maldives, Japan, Italy, Sri Lanka Also try: Namibia Road Trip: Etosha National Park to Fish River Canyon When Tom Barber, Alastair Poulain and Nick Newbury launched Original Travel from a spare bedroom in 2003, their core product was what they called Big Short Breaks. These days, they’ve gone long-haul, and now go by the name of Voyageurs du Monde, having become part of France's leading tailor-made travel company. But the level of service has only developed, with travellers getting everything from airport meet and greets with fast-track service to personalised app itineraries. The group owns a collection of remarkable properties, from the Steam Ship Sudan on the Nile to Gandhi's one-time home in Johannesburg. It also has a global charitable foundation and claims 100 per cent carbon absorption on trips, which makes their excursions extra guilt-free. Key destinations: Worldwide, brief-led exploration on land and sea Signature trip: Your Private African Wilderness Founded in 2017, Joro’s three co-founders bring a unique experience set to their deeply personalised trips, which have included everything from intricate multi-year family sabbaticals, polar and marine research expeditions by private charter, and immersive 'world-as-classroom' adventures tailored entirely from a blank sheet. Duncan Over is ex-Army, but also spent years running horseback safaris in the Okavango Delta; while Justin Packshaw, also ex-Army, has done everything from summiting Everest to reaching the South Pole unsupported using a kite-ski. Managing director Henry Comyn is also the founder of The Conscious Travel Foundation, and he’s behind much of the carbon-neutral B Corp’s eco-seriousness, which includes producing impact reports for every trip. Key destinations: Sahara Desert, Chad, Republic of Congo, Gabon, Angola, sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Latin America, Arctic, Antarctica Signature trip: The Great Migration in Tanzania Also try: The Emperor Penguins of Atka Bay, Antarctica Founded 35 years ago by Calcutta-born, Kenya-raised Nicola Shepherd, the Explorations Company was shouting about conservation and community engagement on our travels before much of the rest of the world was. Its offering is broad, from Japanese family trips to private mobile camping in the Brazilian Amazon, but the primary leaning is towards nature, and staff tend to be genuine regional experts who’ve spent serious time in situ. One per cent of trip fees go to carefully chosen local initiatives, and the company has raised more than $5 million for more than 100 projects and initiatives around the world, from the Sumba Hospitality Foundation to the Zambian Carnivore Programme. Clients can visit community and humanitarian projects, and conservation projects (including spending time with researchers of various species, such as safaris in Mozambique’s Gorongosa wilderness to learn about its pangolin conservation programme) Key destinations: Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Botswana, the Maldives Also try: Wildlife Wonders: from Rwanda to Botswana Born from a blog Tom Cahalan started over a decade ago, Dorsia Travel specialises in bespoke trips to safari and beach destinations – from private islands in the Maldives and the Caribbean to exclusive-use lodges across Africa. Between them, Cahalan and his wife Lucie (who previously worked in management at The Connaught) spend months each year on the ground, staying at properties they recommend to their mostly US-based clients. “What sets us apart is how personal we keep it,” he says. The pair regularly travel with their children, too, meaning they can give first-hand advice on what works for all ages. One recent request was a family’s first safari, which included conservation activities for the children, fine dining in the bush and a sunrise hot air balloon ride over the Mara. Best for: Couples, families and small groups looking for the inside track on Latin America Key destinations: Argentina, Chile, Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador & Galápagos, Bolivia, Uruguay, Venezuela. Mexico, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, Antarctica Signature trip: Road tripping in the Argentine Northwest (Argentina) Also try: Where the Andes meet the Amazon (northern Peru) Founded by former journalist Harry Hastings in Buenos Aires in 2006, Plan South America explores the furthest reaches of Latin America, building an enviable network of guides, conservationists, chefs, artists and local characters along the way. Now operating between London, Buenos Aires and Santiago, the company creates individual private journeys for travellers that go beyond the familiar luxury circuit. With an emphasis on cultural immersion, rare access and meticulous planning, its strength lies in knowing which lodge is worth the detour, which guide will bring a place to life and where to find authenticity. Experiences range from tracking jaguars in Brazil's Pantanal to exploring remote Andean communities and private sailing expeditions through Patagonia and Antarctica. Five Star Greece began in 2004 when Ileana von Hirsch, the daughter of a Greek ship owner, wanted an elegant way to rent out her family’s beautiful Ithaca estate, where Aristotle Onassis and other Greek luminaries would often stop by. Today, Ileana and her team of six experts are Greece’s key travel fixers (they prefer the term matchmaker), with her contacts book conferring insider access to the country’s very best villas and yachts, many of them exclusive and none shared publicly or detailed online. Clients tend to come by word of mouth and stay for the exceptional levels of on-the-ground service, which include building a film set-quality sandy beach and beach bar for a high-profile family and their VIP guests. Best for: Villa holidays, French châteaux, Scottish castles Key destinations: France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Croatia, UK, Caribbean Signature trip: A multigenerational escape to a French château, with private pool, generous grounds, and a private chef Also try: The Water Tower on the Royal Sandringham Estate Founded in 2003 by Oliver Bell and Ravi Sabharwal, the luxury villa specialist Oliver’s Travels seeks to find holiday homes that can be destinations in their own right. Its collection includes more than 8,000 handpicked homes across over 25 countries, with an eye for extraordinary character and a genuine sense of place. French châteaux remain a speciality, alongside centuries-old Italian masserias, private Caribbean islands and Scottish castles worthy of a Traitors-style celebration. The broad collection also caters to families and multigenerational groups planning special celebrations.
