item.title: INSTRUCTION: Collard Greens Vinaigrette
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green. For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes. Step 2Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool. Step 3Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside. Step 4Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside. Step 5Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours. Step 6Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves. Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: 10 ways to use points and miles for a fabulous trip to London
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
London routinely ranks among the world’s most-visited cities. It is home to incredible museums, a fabulous theater scene, great restaurants, luxurious hotels and its main airport, Heathrow (LHR), is a hub for multiple airlines, making it a great stopping-over point on a larger trip. That said, the British capital is well worth visiting on its own for anything from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how much of an Anglophile you are. Despite the strong U.S. dollar, London is still an expensive destination, so if price points have been putting you off lately, here are some easy strategies to stretch your London trip budget even further using miles and points. And if you have some strategies of your own to use airline miles, hotel points and credit card rewards to maximize a trip to London, please share those in the comments below! What is the best area of London to stay in? Where you should stay in London depends on the purpose of your visit. If you are in town for business, you might want to stay near the City of London, while folks who want a quieter neighborhood might like Kensington or Notting Hill. Knightsbridge is best for those who want upscale shopping, while Mayfair has fantastic restaurants and boutiques. When is the best time of year to visit London? London can get dreary and gray during the winter months and crowded during the summer, so your best bets are fall from September-November and spring from March-May when the temperatures tend to be mild and days will include a mix of sun and rain. How many miles does it take to fly to London? The number of miles you need to fly to London depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage programs require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like Virgin Atlantic, by redeeming as few as 6,000 miles each way. What airlines fly to London? American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines all fly to London from various U.S. airports. You’ll also find plenty of flights from over a dozen U.S. cities from the U.K.’s two main carriers, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic. How much does a trip to London cost? The cost of a trip to London depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The city has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury hotels that can cost well over $500 a night. Luckily, many hotels are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points. Now that the FAQs are out of the way, here's what else you need to know to start planning your trip to London. Virgin Atlantic flies to London Heathrow from 11 U.S. cities and using Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points can be a real bargain. Just beware of taxes and fees that can be several hundred dollars, even for economy tickets. I like using the airline’s Reward Seat Checker tool to price out tickets between city pairs over a month at a time. You can often find economy tickets between the East Coast and London for as few as 6,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly — you can cross the Atlantic for just 6,000 miles. Even better, premium economy starts at just 10,500 miles and Upper Class can require as few as 29,000 miles (though it’s often much higher). Unfortunately, you’ll be on the hook for anywhere from $450-$1,700 in taxes and fees round-trip depending on your class of service. That’s a lot, but perhaps not so bad considering even some economy flights are costing upwards of $1,400 at the moment, saving a few hundred dollars by redeeming a few thousand miles can be well worth it. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of: What’s more, some of these partners, including Amex and Bilt, offer limited-time transfer bonuses, so you can score even more of a deal on award tickets. Soften those surcharges on British Airways business class British Airways is one of the most generous airlines in the world when it comes to releasing award seats in its four classes of long-haul service: economy, premium economy, business class and first class. The downside is the hefty fuel surcharges and taxes on the airline's flights to and from its London Heathrow hub. There are, however, some ways to mitigate those. The key is to redeem points and miles from the right programs. The extra charges will still be relatively high, but you can end up saving hundreds of dollars per ticket — each way! To illustrate this most clearly, let's focus on British Airways business class. While American Airlines AAdvantage would only require 57,500 miles each way in business class for British Airways flights between the U.S. and London, the taxes and fees can cost between $750-$1,000 each way. The same is true if you were to redeem 45,000-70,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points each way – with taxes and fees that can top $1,100. Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Flights from the East Coast start at 63,000 miles plus $200-$450 in each direction, while those from the West Coast incur the same taxes and fees, but require 93,000 miles. For its part, British Airways Club would require 88,000-99,000 Avios in each direction depending on which city in the U.S. you’re flying from, plus taxes and fees closer to $400-$500. Yes, that is still a chunk of change, and it’s a lot more Avios or Asia Miles, but it can be well worth it to save close to a thousand dollars per person. British Airways Club is a transfer partner of: Cathay Pacific Asia Miles is a transfer partner of: That means that although you’re spending more miles for a ticket than redeeming through AAdvantage or Atmos, you have a lot more transfer partner options to top up your British Airways or Cathay Pacific accounts. Award ticket savings for United cardholders Another way to save on taxes and fees on award tickets as well as sparing yourself a few miles is to redeem United MileagePlus miles for a ticket on United. Not only does United charge far lower taxes and fees than British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, but if you are either a United MileagePlus elite or carry a United cobranded card, you might be eligible for preferential redemption rates on award tickets booked through MileagePlus. You’ll pay just $5.60 flying from the U.S. to London, in any class of service, and around $200-$400 on the return, depending on which cabin you’re in. Plus, you can save on the mileage portion of your ticket if you’re an elite or a credit cardholder. Take these flights from London to Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), for instance. Regular MileagePlus members would have to redeem 40,000 miles for coach, 50,000 for premium economy and 80,000 for United Polaris business class. But if you have access to preferential rates, you’ll save at least 10% of the miles and need just 36,000 for coach, 45,000 for premium economy and 72,000 for business class. If you don’t currently carry a United credit card, consider the United℠ Explorer Card (see ) or the United Quest℠ Card (see ). United is also a 1:1 transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards if you carry one of the following cards: Finally, don’t forget that United has a special partnership with Marriott. Normally, when you transfer 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to one of its airline partners, you end up with 20,000 airline miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus for 25,000 miles total. With United, however, you get a 10,000-mile bonus, so 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to 30,000 United miles. That’s probably a special-circumstance use for most folks, but still something to consider if you’re swimming in Marriott points. As you might expect, London is lousy with points hotels, and more are on the way. I’m most excited about the Waldorf Astoria London – Admiralty Arch and the St. Regis London, both of which should open in early 2027. I’d suggest picking the area you want to stay in and then doing a search with your preferred hotel programs around there. In the meantime, here are some of my top picks with each program. The swanky NoMad London opened in 2021 and immediately gained a following thanks to its maximalist decor and popular bars and restaurants, not to mention its central Covent Garden location. It’s now part of Hilton, so you can redeem points for stays. Nights start at $550 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points. I also love the colorful BoTree Hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. It opened in a quiet pocket of Mayfair in 2023 and has bright but sophisticated rooms and is home to an outpost of the see-and-be-seen Italian eatery Lavo. Rates start at $400 or 108,000 Hilton Honors points per night. I love Mayfair, so my top Hyatt pick for the city is Hyatt Regency London – The Churchill, which sits right on stately Portman Square and is turning 50 years old next year. The room decor is not exactly overawing, but the public spaces are grand indeed and the service is impeccable. Nights start at $440 or 25,000-55,000 World of Hyatt points per night. TPG staffers also love the Great Scotland Yard Hotel, which is part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rooms are on the small side, but you can’t beat the history since it’s in a heritage-listed building that was once the Metropolitan Police headquarters. Rates start at $380 or 20,000-40,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For something a bit hipper as well as budget-friendlier, try the Standard. It’s in a very busy area right near Kings Cross, but chic, 70s-inspired room decor and several buzzy bars and restaurants will make your time here feel like an upscale city experience. Rates start at $305 or 20,000-40,000 points per night. Even among quirky Kimptons, the Kimpton Fitzroy is a standout thanks to the magnificent 1900 landmark building that houses it and its central Bloomsbury location. Make time for afternoon tea in Palm Court, which is a veritable London institution. Rates start at $319 or 66,000 IHG One Rewards points per night. The InterContinental London Park Lane has an utterly convenient location at Hyde Park Corner and features spacious rooms, specialty drinks inspired by the royal family at Arch Bar and an expansive spa and fitness center. Rates start at $433 or 83,000 points per night. It might occupy a heritage-listed building from 1910, but the London Edition feels utterly of the moment (even though it opened over 13 years ago). Rooms have Edition’s signature look of white textiles, wood paneling and minimalist bathrooms. It’s worth spending an evening admiring the sculpted ceiling at Berners Tavern while enjoying dishes from chef Jason Atherton’s menu. Rates start at $485 or 70,400 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. Formerly a Renaissance hotel, St. Pancras has since joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection and is a favorite among train enthusiasts thanks to its location in a landmark neo-Gothic edifice attached to the train station of the same name. Rooms feel opulent in a Victorian way, and its Moorish-inspired spa is a treat. Rates start at $280 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. Get a third or fourth night free at luxury hotels While hotel points come in handy for saving bundles of money on otherwise expensive stays, if you are looking to splurge while in London, there are still ways to save on luxury hotels. Travelers with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express should check American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, which sometimes has third- or fourth-night free packages at some of the city’s finest hotels. These bookings also come with perks like free daily breakfast for two, a $100 on-property credit, availability-based upgrades and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout. There are plenty to choose from, but my personal favorite London hotels that participate in Amex FHR include: Remember, if you have the American Express Platinum Card or The Business Platinum Card from American Express you are also eligible for up to $300 in statement credits biannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe bookings (of two nights or more for THC and Airbnb) through American Express Travel® or the Amex Travel App™. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, those FHR bookings will require two nights or more to be eligible for this credit. You might also consider booking a luxury hotel through the Capital One Premier Collection if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business for valuable benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available). Likewise, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business you can book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠. Cardholders are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more booked through The Edit. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit. Destination dining from around the world Although British food was long a punchline, the city has become one of the world’s premier dining destinations in the past two decades or so. These days, you can find everything from Sri Lankan hoppers and Scandinavian smoked fish to French haute cuisine and sustainable farm-to-table fare. Prices are high, though, so it’s best to maximize rewards on your spending and any statement credits your credit cards might afford you. Among the ones that might help most are: - Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card: It offers up to $300 (up to $25 per month) in statement credits for purchases at restaurants worldwide and earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases worldwide. - American Express® Gold Card: Earn 4 points per dollar spent on dining at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar). - Chase Sapphire Preferred Card: Earn 3 points per dollar on dining worldwide. - Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 3 points per dollar on dining worldwide. - Citi Strata Premier® Card (see ): Earn 3 points per dollar spent at restaurants. Another favorite tip of mine: You can often find discounts of up to 50% at some restaurants by booking reservations via The Fork. Then, just show your reservation details at check in, enjoy your meal, and the savings will be automatically applied to your bill. Taxis and Ubers are easy to come by in London, though rides can be expensive. So if you do go this route, so to speak, make sure to use a card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services. It’s also easy to hop on the city’s Tube lines and buses, both of which are easy to navigate and affordable, by simply tapping on with your credit card. If you decide to do so, keep a card that earns bonus points on public transportation at the top of your wallet. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) earns 2 points per dollar on local transit and commuting, for example, and the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 2 points per dollar on local transit purchases. You might be able to use the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s $300 in annual travel statement credits toward transit purchases as well as taxis and Ubers since these charges often code as “travel.” No matter whether you spell it “theater” or “theatre,” no trip to London would be complete without seeing a production in one of the West End’s magnificent venues. Ticket prices tend to be more reasonable than in the U.S. but can still put a dent in your budget. Luckily, you can take advantage of the Chase Sapphire Reserve Stubhub credit to offset some of that cost. Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $300 per year to use on purchases made through StubHub or its sister site, Viagogo. The credit is split into two biannual credits of up to $150 (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027). Among the productions currently available through Stubhub in London are “Paddington: The Musical” (just beware it’s mostly sold out except for last-minute tickets) and “Oh, Mary!”. A few years ago, Capital One partnered with The Cultivist, a service that grants members free, priority access to dozens of museums around the world. Eligible Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card holders can register for half-price membership that costs $220 per year instead of $440. This auto-renews at the discounted rate for the second year and then is full price after that. While $220 is a lot, if you visit museums frequently, you can end up saving far more than that on tickets since The Cultivist Enthusiast-level membership available with the Venture X includes priority admission for the cardholder plus a guest. In London, the participating museums include: Finally, some credit cards levy foreign exchange fees on purchases you make outside the U.S. They tend to add 1-3% to your purchase price, which can add up quickly. Instead, use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees, of which there are many to choose from. If you travel abroad frequently, you might also want to consider the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card. In addition to waiving foreign transaction fees, the card actually earns 3 points per dollar on foreign transactions, in any category. It’s almost too good to be true, and that makes it one of the best credit cards for trips abroad.

item.title: PROFILE: NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide
item.description:
Source: Eater
NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo. This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos. At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands. Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from? Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine. Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach. How did you connect with Barrera for the project? Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot... Apolinar: And giving us the flame. Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often. Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership. Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu? Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance. Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that. Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly. How is the service different from your other spots? Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me. Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them? Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there. Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them. item.title: INSTRUCTION: How To Choose a Winter Jacket on Black Friday Without Getting Lost in the Specs
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Shopping for a winter jacket on Black Friday can feel like reading a foreign language. Product pages are filled with terms like fill power, DWR, seam-sealed, and a long list of branded technologies, all promising warmth and protection. With discounts everywhere, it's tempting to grab the jacket with the biggest markdown and hope for the best. But a great price on the wrong jacket is still the wrong jacket. Understanding what those labels mean takes only a few minutes and can help you choose a coat that keeps you comfortable for many winters. Start With Where You'll Actually Wear It Before looking at any specs, think about your typical winter day. A commuter walking between the train and office needs something different from a skier spending hours on the slopes or a parent standing at youth soccer games in freezing drizzle. Dry cold calls for insulation above all. Wet, milder climates need waterproofing more than bulk. Active use like hiking, snowshoeing, or shoveling demands breathability so you don't overheat. Keeping your routine in mind makes every label that follows easier to judge. A good technical jacket is an investment, which is why Black Friday is such a popular time to buy one. Outerwear brands frequently discount their core winter lines in late November, and pairing those markdowns with a promo code can make a higher-performance model surprisingly affordable. If Columbia is on your list, a sensible first step is to check the Columbia listing at Discoup to see whether coupons or promotions are available. You may find extra percentage discounts, free shipping, or offers tied to a minimum spend that bring a warmer or more waterproof jacket within your price range. Treat coupon sources like jacket reviews: one gets you started, and a second site tracking the same brand works as a quick cross-check before you pay. Watch the conditions attached to each code. Some exclude items already marked down, some apply only to full-price collections, and many expire before the long weekend ends. Knowing the rules helps you decide whether to buy on Black Friday, November 27, 2026, or wait for Cyber Monday three days later. Warmth: Down, Synthetic, and Reflective Linings Down insulation is rated by fill power, which measures how much space an ounce of down occupies. Higher numbers (700 or 800 and up) mean more warmth for less weight, while 550 to 650 is typical for everyday jackets. Down is warm and packable but loses much of its insulating ability when wet unless treated to resist moisture. Synthetic insulation is often described in grams, referring to the weight of insulation per square meter. Around 60 grams suits active use or milder days, while 150 grams or more targets serious cold. Synthetics stay warm even when damp and are generally easier to care for. Reflective linings are another approach. Columbia's Omni-Heat technology, recognizable by the metallic dots or pattern inside many jackets, reflects body heat toward you while still letting moisture escape. It could add warmth without much extra bulk. Water: Resistant Is Not the Same as Waterproof This is where many buyers get confused. Water-resistant or water-repellent jackets have a surface treatment (often called DWR, for durable water repellent) that makes light rain bead up and roll off. They handle drizzle and snow flurries but eventually soak through in steady rain. Waterproof jackets use a membrane or coating that blocks water entirely. Waterproof ratings are usually expressed in millimeters: roughly 5,000mm handles moderate rain, while 10,000mm and above is built for heavy, prolonged exposure. Look for seam taping too. Fully taped seams are sealed everywhere, while critically taped means only the most exposed seams are covered. Columbia uses its own names for these features, such as Omni-Tech for waterproof-breathable construction and Omni-Shield for water and stain repellency, so reading the product description helps you tell which level of protection you're getting. A fully waterproof jacket that doesn't breathe can leave you damp inside. Breathability ratings, often given in grams per square meter over 24 hours, indicate how well moisture vapor escapes; higher numbers are better for active use. Pit zips, adjustable cuffs, a helmet-compatible or insulated hood, and a longer cut that covers your hips can matter just as much as the headline technology. The best Black Friday jacket isn't the one with the flashiest discount but the one whose features match how you spend your cold days. Decide how you'll use it, decode the labels, check that the insulation and waterproofing fit your climate, and then let a good sale and a carefully selected code do the rest. You'll end up with a jacket that feels like a smart purchase every time the temperature drops. This story was published in partnership with Discoup.

item.title: Does Anti-Stink Clothing Actually Work? We (Really) Wanted to Find Out
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
I boarded a 3-hour flight wearing a T-shirt I’d worn for over three weeks straight. By this point I only had a vague sense of what I smelled like. Sleeping bag sweat? Iso gas? Hot dog water? I listened to the crew make the “very full flight” announcement again and shifted in my middle seat. It wasn’t just that I had a dirty shirt on—I’d barely showered for the entire trip, and apart from a few bracing dips in rivers and ocean water, I had made little effort to clean myself at all. Instead, techy fabrics from Patagonia and an innovative startup called HercLéon battled my oils and odors at point-blank. Except for deodorant, all that guarded the packed flight from trail stank were various items of “laundry-free” or “anti-odor” clothing. My Patagonia pants and sun hoodie were treated with steam-extracted, food-grade mint oil. The HercLéon T-shirt and my boxer briefs were infused with charcoal and woven with copper fibers. I had used exfoliating nylon washcloths from Lunatec that “never need washing.” Had it worked? When I planned to hike through the majority of Washington state on a former rail grade, I immediately thought it would be helpful to bring only one set of clothes. But if I tried it and anything went wrong, I could be exposed. As is the case on many long-distance hikes, I knew clothes shopping could be a tough ask depending on where I was. Still, wardrobe weight is real, and weight quickly becomes the enemy of comfort. So could materials like Patagonia’s HeiQ and HercLeon’s HercCopper limit foul smells after days on trail? Could that improve my overall mood, along with the weight savings, and could it all help me with social graces along the way? My target was a 330-mile segment of the Great American Rail Trail. It links old railroad corridors from the western Cascades to the Idaho border, dividing roughly into two halves that mirror Washington’s geography: rugged mountains west of the Columbia River and sparse deserts to the east. I quickly realized small-town hospitality would be my only ticket through the eastern deserts. With no infrastructure or known water on the trail for 40 miles in some areas, networking with anyone willing to provide would be key. I knew I’d be more likely to score overnight stays or solid hookups if I didn’t roll into town smelling like Sasquatch. Early on, though, the hike took a hard turn: I limped off the trail after 60 miles with a foot injury, but decided to stay in Washington anyway. Some supportive offers from friends could give me a runway to rest up until my original bail date, and maybe hit some rock climbing if I could recover in time. Because that plan would still require a pretty deep level of dirtbagging, I knew I could keep stink-testing my clothes—which had amazed me to this point. The accident led to a variety of activities I wasn’t planning on. This demanded resilience and adaptation from me and everything in my kit, including my clothes. Apart from activities, my clothing was also subjected to heavy chemical factors, including sleeping bag sweat, dehydrated meal sweat, fried food sweat, and beer sweat. Smoky campsites, rampant use of catholes and wag bags, many cups of coffee, and trash bags packed in vans directly alongside gear during rainy spells also played a role. In short, I believe the textile engineering of several items made it possible to keep the same clothes on my back for the duration—without disgusting myself, visibly offending service workers, or prompting any business owners to kick me out. To understand this question is to understand why a tiny startup like HercLéon would market a copper-infused T-shirt for $130. TL;DR: Body odor happens because our skin is a Golden Corral for bacteria. And it’s open 24 hours. No matter what we’re doing, our skin is always generating natural oils and shedding dead cells. Glands in areas like the armpits and groin constantly leech thicker protein- and lipid-composed fluids onto the skin. The resulting buildup becomes a body-sized feeding trough for potentially trillions of bacteria. When those bacteria expel waste, that’s where stink comes from. That and the layers of old oil, decaying cells, etc. that accumulate until you wash them off with soap and water. Imagine flooding this system with sweat, then draping a layer of clothing on top. Sweat itself is generally odorless, but it does help bacteria multiply. And when it touches the clothing, it allows them to swim, slosh, or spill over. If your skin is a microbial Golden Corral, your sweaty clothes are like a swim-up bar attached to the dining room. But not all textiles are equally hospitable. Polyester repels water but attracts oil. Skin oils can bond tightly to its synthetic fibers, but the fibers naturally reject water, even in the washing machine. The oil, and anything else gummed up in it, gets welded to the fabric. (This is why some of your cheapest workout shirts get “permastink.”) Merino wool is the opposite: It repels oil and attracts water. The thirsty fibers soak up sweat from the skin, but leave most bacteria behind, stuck in the oil. And because the merino is removing their water source, the bacteria have a harder time multiplying and farting out more odor. Techy fabrics like those from Patagonia and HercLéon take this equation of moisture and bacterial transfer to the nth degree—they seek to wall off the swim-up bar. The HercShirt felt great right out of the bag in a size small, and matched my sizing expectations. Field performance proved to be incredible. The fabric felt slightly heavy, sliding across my skin with a gentle pressure that felt cooling and was never scratchy. I found it fit closely enough to help me look sharp in town, but it never lost its shape. After three weeks, the material still felt stretchy everywhere. The collar hadn’t bagged out, and even the shirt’s hem under my hip belt wasn’t sagging or creased. By the end of the journey, it was tie-dyed with sweat stains from pack straps, but still passed as a deep navy blue. It never developed pit stains. Of course, odor did become noticeable. It’s hard to say whether it was on day 12 or 20, but I also made no effort to clean the shirt. So based on my testing, HercLeon’s stated 10-day freshness target is fair—especially if you take the punishing factors of my testing field into account. My shirt endured days of sweaty hiking, exposure to muggy northwestern rainforests, late nights out on the town, cold snaps, and rainstorms that kept me layered up for days on end. It survived nights wadded up at the bottom of a sleeping bag around my heinous feet. I have almost no doubt that 10 days of normal wear with regular showers would be feasible. My HercUnderwear 2.0 Boxer Briefs were equally impressive. With the caveat that there is a wide spectrum of underwear hygiene tolerance in the population, my findings are below. First, did I wear the same pair of underwear every day for over three weeks without washing them? No, because there are bacterial realities that command respect. I did take a backup pair of boxer briefs, and I wrung out the HercUnderwear once in a sink with hand soap and once in the ocean. With only this spartan care, the single pair of shorts served for up to nine days at a time. (I used wet wipes consistently.) For comparison, I did test how long I could make my spare Hanes 92/8 poly/spandex units last. I found four days was my threshold, and wanted to incinerate them after that for the benefit of the trash workers. Meanwhile, crude handwashing rejuvenated the HercUnderwear to a satisfactory extent for the field. I found fit and roominess to be on the small side. I opted for medium with my 29-30” waist. Ultimately, I’ll keep the underwear in my kit for activities except hot-weather hiking. The fabric is a bit heavier than many boxer briefs, and can feel slightly warming depending on pants choice. HercLéon’s engineering exists at every level of manufacturing. Instead of using a spray-on coating, the brand mixes tiny particles of copper and charcoal into its raw textile material before spinning that into fibers. It is called a “masterbatch.” Materials are chosen to control odor at three different points: bacterial growth, odor absorption, and moisture management. The shirt starts with lyocell, a soft, moisture-absorbing textile fiber made from processed wood pulp. Copper particles embedded in the fibers release antimicrobial ions when damp. This damages bacterial cell walls, limiting their ability to multiply and convert sweat and other food sources into foul-smelling compounds. The next contingency is charcoal. Their highly porous carbon structure can trap odor molecules that do develop, HercLéon says, preventing them from escaping into the air. Finally, “plasma modification”—altering the surface properties of the fibers with ionically-charged gases during manufacturing—causes sweat to spread out and evaporate across the garment, rather than accumulate. Less lingering moisture means fewer opportunities for bacteria to multiply. HercLéon recently launched the HercSock 5 on Kickstarter, which uses the same technology that’s in the shirt and the boxer briefs. However, I did not get to test them on this trip. Stumbling into Cle Elum, Washington, with wobbly legs, an injured foot, and a calorie deficit, I lurched toward the nearest bar (a long, long mile away). It had been a 30-mile day, and I’d been walking since it was too cold to feel my fingers in the morning. The afternoon in the sparse Yakima River valley had reached 93 degrees. I hadn’t stopped to change clothes—I knew I was hurt and no comfort would amount to real relief. Night fell, and I sat down at a park bench in a fugue state to put on layers. I reached for my shirt collar to pull it off, expecting to wrestle with a sweat-soaked sheet. Instead, it was bone dry. My Patagonia Capilene Cool Ultra hoody slotted into the “go-to” position on the trip. The lightest of four entries in the Capilene line, Patagonia builds it specifically for summer temperatures. I confirmed this use case in an unseasonably hot, exposed ascent of the west face of Exfoliation Dome. But I also discovered the hoody had just enough weight to take the shiver factor out of a damp Pacific morning. Features are limited but functional. I found that using the thumb loops didn’t stretch the sleeves beyond recognition, and I liked the single button to tighten the hood. There are no pockets. Wearing the hoody roughly as much as my HercShirt, often layered with it, I got the sense that odor control wasn’t quite as strong. But it did still generally meet the limits of social acceptability by the end of the trip. And since it was easy to rinse and dried fast, I had no problem dunking it and wringing it occasionally. According to Patagonia’s anti-stink coating provider, this shouldn’t have worked to refresh odor-fighting capabilities. The coating is a handful of botanicals arranged in a bioengineered structure. HeiQ Mint contains essential mint oils and other “naturally derived deodorizing ingredients”—inside capsules the manufacturer claims are capable of trapping the oils and acids that cause odor. This proprietary “encapsulation technology” snatches odor-causing particles and encloses them during wear. Then it releases them during washing thanks to the alkalinity of soapy water. Thus, laundering duds like the Capilene Cool hoody restores them for their next use, according to HeiQ. On the last day of the trip, we walked down from the base of Blueberry Buttress (5.8+, 1,000 feet). In just a half mile from the foot of the climb to the car, we lost 1,300 feet of elevation. Quads screaming, we reached my borrowed van and flopped. My climbing partner wrestled himself out of his soaking wet T-shirt, now two or three sizes too big, and hung it on a tree branch. My Capilene hoody wasn’t stinking up the campsite, and it still fit around my shoulders. Plus, it was dry enough to continue wearing comfortably. Lunatec’s “never needs washing” camp cloths were absolutely clutch in my kit. With no technology on board except a loose weave for fast drying, the two units thoroughly supplemented wiping and cleanup needs without creating their own. The green “odor-free” dishcloth was abrasive enough to lift stuck-on burnt bits, and highly durable. Its diffuse weave made it economical to rinse after scouring cookware with sand. The “self-cleaning” washcloth, slightly larger and stretchier, played well for more detailed work. It was minimally absorbent (I didn’t reach for it when I spilled an entire beer into my friend’s van carpet). But viscous bits like snot or soup remnants clung to it well, then vanished when rinsed. The elastic hang tabs doubled as gathering straps, making each cloth easy to pack up. What is Lunatec’s secret to self-cleaning? According to the brand, nothing. Their washcloths are 100% nylon, and nothing else. A backpacker’s world is a stinky one no matter what. So if you’re on an anti-gross-out program, how can you tell if your efforts have meant anything? How can you tell if you’ve kept the Golden Corral in the corral? There is a device used to measure odors in clinical settings called an olfactometer. It works by, basically, establishing a control smell and then upping the ante in increments—approaching the threshold where the subject can’t handle it anymore. In everyday practice, though, you experience moments when you become suddenly aware of an odor. You lift a shoulder to reach an awkward zipper or squat fast to pick up something you dropped—and the wave breaks. A solid mass of stink floods your face, and you wonder how long everyone else has been able to tell. For many of us, that’s the trigger. “I need to wash, somehow, now.” Over 25 days living in a pretty dirty corner of the dirtbag life, I never had that moment. River plunges sufficed for bathing. Sink water rinses refreshed the hardest workhorses in my wardrobe. I didn’t take a microscope, but I think the makers of my clothing delivered on their broad promise: Science can help you not stink (or at least, stink less). The maintenance burden of living outside full-time had been meaningfully decreased. I thrived in my unexpected program of outdoor and social events for over three weeks with a wardrobe that would fit in a McDonald’s bag, and I’d spent zero time doomscrolling at the laundromat. Boarding my flight, I looked down at my disheveled rags and scratched at an itch in my neck—I also hadn’t shaved for the whole trip. Then, both of my neighbors arrived and settled in, smiled warmly, and relaxed.

item.title: IDEA: What Time Should You Eat Thanksgiving Dinner?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Every family has Thanksgiving rules. Some are spoken (“Dinner’s at 3 sharp!”), others understood (Mom gets the wings), and plenty are hotly contested. We asked Bon Appétit staffers, friends, and their kids to settle the holiday’s thorniest questions. Turns out, there’s no one right way to Thanksgiving—just plenty of opinions. What makes a good guest? If you don’t cook, you’d better clean! —Meredith, 41, Golden Rule follower As someone who hosts, I have a system, and I want everyone to stay out of my way. —Catherine, 41, channeling inner peace My mom makes me dust everything. And be honest, no one is going to see the baseboards. —Alice, 8, at your service (begrudgingly) Guests should bring dessert or flowers. Let me figure out the wine! —Rachel, 41, future somm What’s the dress code? You need to look nice for Grandma. —David, 48, upstanding gentleman Bring out the stretchy pants! —Haleigh, 31, comfort queen Turkey costume. —Max, 9, gobble-gobbling Brown sweater and, like, beige pants. —Amanda, 12, loves a uniform When should we eat? What’s on the menu? There has to be turkey. —Ashley, 43, traditionalist Instead of sides we should have doughnuts and Cheetos and cakes. —Charlie, 10, angling for leftovers Who gets the first slice of pie? Just do your best. —Synge, 28, here for moral support The grown-ups eat and talk and the kids eat as fast as they can so they can go play in the other room. —Charlie, 10, ready for the Turkey Trot

item.title: REVIEW: Review: Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is an ultralight, close-fitting base layer designed for high-output cold-weather activities. It is made with Octa Fleece, a warm, highly breathable ultralight fleece similar to Polartec Alpha Direct, but much more durable, and pairs well with a windbreaker or winter shell jacket. If you’re not familiar with Mountain Equipment, they’re a highly regarded British manufacturer that has designed technical outdoor gear for mountaineering and polar exploration since 1961. They make a wide range of products, including technical clothing, sleeping bags, and mountaineering backpacks. Backcountry.com carries their products in the United States. I’ve been recommending Mountain Equipment’s men’s Ibex and women’s Chamois softshell pants for winter hiking for years, and they’re still best in class. The top uses 20-denier, 100% Octa Fleece, made from a specialized hollow polyester fiber with eight radial projections that give the yarn a gear- or octopus-like cross-section. The hollow center and projecting “fins” create insulating air spaces that trap warm air, letting water vapor escape. Octa Fleece has a similar warmth-to-weight ratio as Polartec Alpha Direct but is more durable, which is why larger clothing manufacturers such as Arc’teryx and Mountain Hardwear use it and are developing products with it. See our FAQ for a more detailed comparison of Octa Fleece and Polartec Alpha Direct. The inside of the Switch Base Zip-T is a fuzzy, warm fabric that is a delight to wear next to the skin or over a thin base layer, while the outer surface is made of highly breathable, abrasion-resistant mesh. The Switch Base Zip-T can be worn as a base layer or a mid-layer over a thin base. The interior has a fuzzy fleece texture that feels warm and comfortable. Flatlocked seams improve next-to-skin comfort by reducing bulk and minimizing potential irritation. The exterior is an open and breathable mesh that is much more abrasion-resistant. Thumbhole loops help keep the sleeves in place when adding a midlayer or waterproof shell. Nylon shoulder overlays protect an area that sees regular friction from backpack straps. This added reinforcement improves the top’s suitability for regular mountain use without significantly compromising its lightweight design. A deep half-zip provides practical ventilation when body heat builds, making the Switch Base Zip T more adaptable than a standard crew-neck baselayer. Similarly, the loose wrists let you pull the sleeves up your arms to vent more heat. I’ve found the Switch to be a delightful base and mid-layer, worn by itself or under a windbreaker on a chilly morning. The fabric is more wind-resistant than a mid-layer hoodie made with Polartec Alpha Direct, and I like using a pullover like it in winter more than a hoodie because it’s easier to layer with the shells and headgear (hats) I typically wear. Best Uses for the Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T The Switch Base Zip T is designed for a wide range of cold-weather activities, including: It performs best during activities that involve frequent changes in effort and temperature since you can vent it so easily or layer it with a windbreaker or shell to increase wind resistance and heat retention. It also delivers warmth well above its weight, making it a lightweight midlayer that packs an outsized amount of warmth. The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is a well-designed cold-weather or winter base layer for active users who prioritize low weight, quick drying, and effective ventilation. Its Octa Fleec fabric provides lightweight warmth while helping manage moisture, and the half-zip makes it easy to regulate temperature during demanding climbs and ski tours. It is not the best choice for maximum insulation when activity levels are low, but that is not its main purpose. For fast-moving winter adventures, the combination of comfortable seams, reinforced shoulders, and quick-drying performance makes the Switch Base Zip T a strong and practical choice. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Disclosure: Mountain Equipment donated a garment for review.

item.title: “Should I Jump? Should I Not Jump?” How Resisting Panic Saved a Climber Stuck on a One Foot Ledge
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
New York State forest rangers conduct an overnight rope rescue on Mount Colden in the Adirondack Mountains after climber Eric Le Bourhis became stranded on an icy rock slide near the Trap Dike on October 21, 2026. (Photo: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation) A 60-year-old Canadian climber was rescued from New York’s Adirondack Mountains on October 22 after spending seven hours standing on a frozen patch of rock and ice no bigger than a coffee table waiting for search and rescue. For the climber, named Eric Le Bourhis, that miserably stationary wait made him a model subject for rescuers. Le Bourhis was climbing Mount Colden, a 4,714-foot peak near Lake Placid, when he encountered ice and stopped to put on his crampons, the rescue report said. But the bag containing them slipped away and slid down the mountainside, leaving him without the traction he needed to climb any higher. Worse, the wet rock he’d climbed earlier was now frozen, making it too slippery to descend. Le Bourhis was effectively trapped. There was a cluster of trees just seven feet away offering a possible escape, but reaching them meant risking a potentially deadly jump across the icy slope. In a video interview released by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Le Bourhis said he resisted the temptation to jump, a decision that spared him the risk of a potentially deadly fall. “I agonized over that, should I try to jump this gap? Should I jump? Should I not jump? Should I activate the beacon? Finally, when I saw the sun was setting, I decided to activate the beacon,” he said. And according to Chris Boyer, executive director of the National Association for Search and Rescue, it’s precisely those moments of desperation that can turn an already dangerous situation into something much worse. “The more you move, the more desperate you get, and the worse the decisions you make are,” Boyer told Outside. “You start to take on more risk about, can I make it across this stream? Can I climb this area? Things like that. So we want to minimize their risk and maximize their survivability and findability,” he said. Le Bourhis was climbing a route known as the Trap Dike, which winds through a steep, rocky passage on Mount Colden before opening onto broad, exposed slopes near the summit. He had climbed it before. Classified as a Class 4 climb, the route requires using both hands and feet, and a fall can be fatal. After dropping his crampons, Le Bourhis activated his satellite distress beacon as the sun went down. Dispatch received the signal at 6:22 P.M., but Le Bourhis didn’t know whether help was coming. With no room to sit, he spent the next seven hours standing and trying to keep his increasingly tired legs steady. “I wanted to entertain myself by looking at Lake Placid, or maybe the lights of people coming for me,” he said. “But I didn’t even have that as entertainment because it made me a bit wobbly. So I just put my headlamp on low and looked at the ground right in front of me for hours and tried to stay upright.” When panic sets in, stranded travelers often convince themselves that help isn’t coming and that they will starve or freeze before anyone notices they are gone, Boyer told Outside. “That flight response kicks in,” Boyer said. “All those things start to manifest, and that can do weird things to you. You think, ‘Nobody’s going to come find me, no one knows I’m missing, and the only way for me to survive is to walk out on my own.'” Staying put is not an absolute rule, of course. Boyer clarified that travelers facing immediate dangers, such as avalanches or lightning, may need to move to safety. Absent an immediate threat, however, remaining stationary gives rescuers a reliable starting point without worrying that someone has wandered into an area they’ve already searched. Forest rangers reached Le Bourhis at 1:16 A.M. on October 22. One ranger ventured onto the icy slope to secure him to a rope system before the team guided him into the trees. A punishing bushwhack uphill and a trail descent followed before the operation ended at 8 A.M., nearly 14 hours after his initial SOS. Forest Ranger Nate Jeffery, who helped rescue Le Bourhis, described the climber as unusually well prepared, despite the mistakes that had left him stranded. “I don’t think there’s too many subjects that could pull off the composure to stay calm and collected and maintain their position on that ledge for that long,” Jeffery said in a separate DEC video interview. Despite carrying an emergency beacon, Le Bourhis never imagined he’d be the one calling for help. “I felt a huge rush of guilt and shame,” he said. “Well, why did I have a beacon then? I don’t know. But I never thought I would have to use it.” Boyer says backcountry users should always feel free to call for help during an emergency. Volunteer teams devote their time, money, and training to helping people in trouble, he said. “Ninety-nine percent of search and rescue personnel in the U.S. are volunteer. They live for this,” he said. ” They beg for this. They train hard. They get certifications. They spend personal money on gear. They prepare for this, and they want to help. They’re an altruistic service that’s available, and don’t feel bad about calling them.”
